notes.text: The forward lines keep changing. Even their four most-used trios over the last 10 games cover only 31% of their forwards’ 5-on-5 time, the fourth-lowest in the league (a typical team: 42%). The lines listed lean on their latest games, but expect new combinations tonight.
Artemi Panarin is away for personal reasons and has missed the last 3 games. He is one of their most valuable skaters. Alex Turcotte has taken his spot beside Adrian Kempe and Alex Laferriere.
Trevor Moore is day to day and missed their last game.
Chris Kreider is out (lower body injury) and has missed the last 4 games.
Josh Anderson is out about 3-4 weeks (lower body injury) and has missed the last 3 games.

Mike Matheson is out about 3-4 weeks (lower body injury) and has missed the last 4 games. He is a top-four defenseman. Alexandre Carrier has taken his spot beside Kaiden Guhle. That pair has had 38% of the chances at 5-on-5 in 33:41 together, down from 54% with Matheson.
Brett Berard was added to the roster on Nov 16 and has played beside Oliver Kapanen and Owen Beck.
Oliver Kapanen is no longer killing penalties: 1% of the team’s shorthanded time in 16 games, down from 33% last season.
Arber Xhekaj has started killing penalties: on the ice for 29% of the team’s shorthanded time in 22 games, up from 6% last season.

stakes: The Kings go in seventh in the Pacific with 16 points, the Canadiens tied for first in the Atlantic with 32 points.

MTL.head: Anybody’s game
MTL.body: Los Angeles has been out-chancing opponents lately, but Montréal has home-ice advantage, and the Kings will be without Panarin. For the Canadiens, the difference could be piling up shots.

LAK.head: Too close to call
LAK.body: Los Angeles has been out-chancing opponents lately, but Montréal has home-ice advantage, and the Kings will be without Panarin. For the Kings, the difference could be a penalty kill that holds up.

story.head: The matchup inside the matchup
paras: Both teams have won two in a row. Going in, the Kings are seventh in the Pacific (tied for 28th in the NHL) and the Canadiens second in the Atlantic (tied for fourth).

The Kings have played better than their record (.400) says: their chances are worth about .615, and their finishing has held them back. The Canadiens’ record (.696) is running ahead of what their chances are worth (.548), largely because they’re 9-5 in one-goal games.

The Kings leave the shooting to their forwards (2nd lowest) and hound the puck on the forecheck (5th). They also keep dangerous shots away better than anyone (1st), so the Canadiens’ good looks will be harder to come by against them. The Habs get into more chippy games than almost anyone (2nd) and have had some of the best goaltending in the league (4th), but take more penalties than they draw (31st). Put that together and the Canadiens’ defensemen shoot a lot, and the Kings’ not so much.

Adrian Kempe (6 G / 8 A / 14 P in 19 GP) is tied for the Kings’ scoring lead. Alex Laferriere (4 G / 10 A / 14 P in 20 GP) shares it. For the Canadiens, Lane Hutson (5 G / 19 A / 24 P in 23 GP) leads the way in scoring, and Cole Caufield (12 G / 8 A / 20 P in 23 GP) has a team-high twelve goals.

Darcy Kuemper (7-5-1 / .885 SV% in 13 GS) will likely start for Los Angeles. Montréal has two options in net: Jacob Fowler (10-2-2 / .924 SV% in 14 GS) and Jakub Dobeš (4-3-2 / .864 SV% in 9 GS). Fowler has started seven of their last ten games, so expect him back in net after Dobeš got the last one on Thursday.

items.text: The Kings are newly without Artemi Panarin and Trevor Moore.
The Canadiens are newly without Josh Anderson, and have been without Chris Kreider, Samuel Montembeault and Mike Matheson for several games.
Juraj Slafkovský has two goals on chances worth about 8.2 goals, well below what his finishing usually turns chances into. If the chances keep coming, so should the goals.
Erik Gustafsson has a point in four straight games.
